children: OTTAWA--Canada's goods-trade surplus with the world shrank sharply in July with the largest retreat in U.S.-bound exports in more than a year and despite signs efforts to pivot to new markets are paying off.

Canadian exports overall fell for the first time since January, retreating from a record high the month before, while imports rose a sixth straight month to the highest level on record. This came ahead of what it expected to be fresh volatility in Canadian trade after an escalation in tensions between Ottawa and Washington and a fresh round of tariffs and countermeasures.

Canada recorded a merchandise-trade surplus in July of 769 million Canadian dollars, the equivalent of about US$555.5 million, Statistics Canada said Thursday. That marked a fifth consecutive surplus but the narrowest of the run, following an upwardly revised C$4.2 billion surplus in June.
Economists were expecting a surplus of C$3.25 billion.
Exports of Canadian goods declined 2.3% between June and July to C$76.14 billion, while the value of imports rose 2.2% to C$75.37 billion, the national data agency said.

Given the pattern of trade early last year after the Trump administration threatened then imposed tariffs aimed at imports from Canada, analysts expect to see efforts to front-run new U.S. levies show up in August trade figures before weighing on exports the next month.

"July trade figures, while disappointing, are largely a look in the rearview mirror as the trade landscape shifted, again, in the following months," Shelly Kaushik, senior economist at Bank of Montreal Capital Markets, said.

President Trump midway through July threatened Canada with new 50% tariffs on a range of goods representing about 5% of exports to the U.S., then introduced the levies late last month after trade talks between the countries broke down. Prime Minister Mark Carney's government plans to retaliate with a tariff package of its own, with duties ranging from 15% to 50% on an equivalent value of U.S. goods, effective next Tuesday.

Canadian shipments to the U.S. sank 6.6% in July, the sharpest pullback since April last year, driven by lower crude oil and gold, prices for which were down during the month. A rise in inbound passenger cars and light trucks helped lift imports from the U.S. by 1.8%. That resulted in the lowest goods-trade surplus with Canada's largest trading partner by far since February at C$5.91 billion from June's C$10.28 billion.

Still, exports to countries other than the U.S. were up 7.4%, a third increase in a row to reach a record high, while imports from non-U.S. countries were up 2.8%. This led to a narrowed trade deficit of C$5.14 billion with countries other than the U.S., the lowest since January 2021.

Carney's government has been working to pivot Canada away from a reliance on the U.S. and strengthen the economy, with a goal of doubling non-U.S. exports over the next decade. Goods exports to non-U.S. countries have increased about 56% since January last year and the proportion of exports bound for the U.S. has declined to roughly 66% from three-quarters of overall shipments historically.

July's fall in total exports was the first in six months and a pullback from a record-high a month earlier, led by declines in metal and mineral products and energy products. Excluding those two segments, exports rose 0.6% for the latest month.

After a nearly 16% jump in June, exports of metals and minerals fell 8.5%, driven by a fall in precious metals that was mainly due to a drop in purchases of Canadian-held gold by foreign residents and fewer shipments to the U.S. and a lower price for the precious metal.

Energy exports were down 4.4% in July, a third consecutive decline as crude fell thanks to lower prices and volumes. Exports of natural gas were also sharply lower after rising the two previous months.

Trade flows were a big driver of the rebound in Canadian activity in the second quarter, with the rise in exports in recent months alongside resilient household spending helping fuel annualized growth of 3.3%, the strongest in about three years. Still, pressures have again built up that threaten to mute economic growth as fuel prices remain elevated and with new tariffs.

In volume terms, overall exports were down 1.5% between June and July, and imports on the same basis were up 2.2%. That indicates net trade was a drag on gross domestic product at the start of the third quarter.

"For the third quarter as a whole, exports may be a slight negative for GDP following the large positive contribution in the second quarter, and could continue to struggle in the fourth quarter unless a trade deal with the U.S. is reached," Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC Capital Markets, said.
